Let $\mathcal{M}$ denote a pre-trained large language model that receives a textual prompt $X$ as input. 
The input $X$ is tokenized into a sequence of tokens $X=\{x_1,..., x_n,..., x_N\}$ where $N$ is the sequence length. 
At each transformer layer $l\in[1,L]$, the hidden representation of token $x_n$ is denoted as the bold item $\bm{x}_n^{(l)}$, with $\bm{X}^{(l)} = [\bm{x}_1;...;\bm{x}_N]$ representing the full input feature matrix at layer $l$. 
For notational simplicity, the layer superscript is omitted ($\bm{x}_n, \bm{X}$) when discussing operations within a single layer. 

External knowledge $\mathcal{G}$ is provided as a set of triples, we use $Z \in \mathcal{G}$ to denote a specific textual triple from a knowledge graph, \eg (\textit{NeurIPS\_2025, held\_in, San Diego}). 
% and it will be also tokenized into a sequence of triple tokens $Z=\{z_1,..., z_m,..., z_M\}$ by $\mathcal{M}$. 
Our goal is to develop an integration mechanism that could dynamically incorporate these triple knowledge into the forward computation of $\mathcal{M}$ to enhance its ability to generate the desired output $Y^*$ in response to the input $X$. 
% Formally, we aim to improve the knowledge fusion process:
% \begin{equation}
%     P(Y^*|X,Z;\bm{\Theta}) = \prod_{t=1}^{|Y^*|} P(y^*|y^*_{<t},X,\mathcal{G};\bm{\Theta})
% \end{equation}
% where $\bm{\Theta}$ denotes model parameters. 
% Specifically, our core innovation lies in the knowledge-guided attention mechanism, which establishes bidirectional interactions between input $\bm{X}$ and external knowledge $\bm{Z}$ representations, while preserving $\mathcal{M}$'s native parameters.

\subsection{Bidirectional Information Aggregation: An Overview}
To achieve the knowledge fusion goal, our primary contribution lies in the introduction of \textit{knowledge graph-guided attention} module, which rewires the original self-attention module via establishing two extra synergistically enhanced information aggregation flows between input $X$ and external knowledge $\mathcal{G}$, while preserving $\mathcal{M}$'s native parameters. 
%
Specifically, these two flows include: 
(1) \textbf{Outward Aggregation Pathway} (Input$\to$KG) dynamically injects external information into the input representations via the attention querying from $X$ to $\mathcal{G}$. This pathway is termed ``\textit{outward}'' as it focuses on the fusion of ``\textit{external}'' knowledge. % through proactive graph retrieval. 
(2) \textbf{Inward Aggregation Pathway} (KG$\to$Input) strategically recalibrates input representations using the semantics of external knowledge, amplifying knowledge-critical patterns while suppressing irrelevant features. %through structured attention reweighting. 
This pathway is designated ``\textit{inward}'' due to its emphasis on ``\textit{input}'' reorganization guided by external knowledge. 
Notably, the arrow notation $\to$ specifically denotes the aggregation directionality, indicating the process of using source representations to reorganize target features, rather than data flow dependencies. 
% Figure~\ref{fig:kga} visually presents these two pathways in our proposed KGA. 
Crucially, both interactions operate through parameter-preserving key-value transformations, avoiding any architectural modifications or new learnable parameters.
Additionally, the framework retains the original ``self''-attention flow (input$\to$input) as the foundational pathway to preserve the model's intrinsic language modeling capabilities of $X$, forming a cohesive tri-flow architecture (see Figure~\ref{fig:kga}). %visualized
% As visualized in Figure~\ref{fig:kga}, this tri-flow architecture - integrating endogenous self-attention with bidirectional knowledge interactions - creates a balanced unification of input information and external knowledge. 
% Figure~\ref{fig:kga} visually presents these two pathways in our proposed KGA. 
% This synergistic design ensures continuous knowledge-text co-evolution across transformer layers while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to standard self-attention implementations. 


% Our framework establishes two novel information aggregation pathways to dynamically utilize structured knowledge while preserving the original modeling capabilities. 
% The first pathway, \textbf{Input$\to$KG aggregation}, projects input representations to query and retrieve relevant information from the knowledge graph, effectively injecting external factual knowledge into the attention computation. 
% This pathway is called \textbf{outward aggregation} since it aims to fuse the external information. 
% The second pathway, \textbf{KG$\to$Input aggregation}, leverages knowledge graph representations to recalibrate input information, systematically amplifying knowledge-aware patterns while suppressing noise or input-irrelevant features through structured input reorganization.
% This pathway is named \textbf{inward aggregation} due to its focus on the input re-organization. 
% Specifically, in these two pathways, the arrows ``$\to$'' do not indicate the relationship of information sources, but rather the mutual interaction relationship, that is, using $A$ to aggregate $B$ for $A\to B$. 
% %
% Crucially, both aggregation pathways operate through key-value matrix interaction rather than introducing new parameters, thereby fully preserving the original model capacities. 
% Additionally, our framework also retains the conventional self-attention flow (Input$\to$Input) as the fundamental pathway, ensuring sustained preservation of intrinsic language understanding capabilities. 
% As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:kga}, this tri-flow architecture – combining internal self-attention with bidirectional knowledge interactions – establishes a synergistic fusion of parametric knowledge and structured symbolic information. 


\subsection{Input\texorpdfstring{$\to$}{lambda}KG (Outward) Aggregation: External Knowledge Fusion}\label{sec:flow1}
This pathway's primary function is to dynamically integrate external information through input-driven knowledge aggregation. 
For a given triple $Z$, we first transform its string-form texts\footnote{We directly input the textual triple (\eg (\textit{NeurIPS\_2025, held\_in, San Diego})) to avoid error introduction from triple-to-text generation, due to their demonstrated capability of understanding triplet knowledge \cite{wang2025kblam,DBLP:journals/kbs/DaiHWSJQ25}.} into continuous $D$-dimensional hidden features through the embedding layer, generating \textit{knowledge representations}. 
These representations are subsequently fused into input features via our KGA layer by layer. 
Formally, we demonstrate the fusion process using the $l$-th layer's KGA (layer index $l$ omitted in the feature matrix for clarity): 
\begin{equation}
    \bm{Q}^Z = \bm{Z} \bm{W}^Q, \quad
    \bm{K}^Z = \bm{Z} \bm{W}^K, \quad
    \bm{V}^Z = \bm{Z} \bm{W}^V
\label{eq:kg-embed}
\end{equation}
where $\bm{Z}$ denotes the feature matrix of external knowledge triple $Z$ containing sequential knowledge token representation $[\bm{z}_1,..., \bm{z}_m,..., \bm{z}_M]$, with $M$ representing the token count in triple $Z$. 
The derived components $\bm{q}^Z_m \in \bm{Q}^Z$, $\bm{k}^Z_m \in \bm{K}^Z$ and $\bm{v}^Z_m \in \bm{V}^Z$ respectively denote the query, key and value features of the $m$-th triple token. 
Crucially, $\bm{W}^Q$, $\bm{W}^K$ and $\bm{W}^V$ are the original weight matrices in the self-attention module\footnote{Direct parameter reuse ensures feature space alignment and architectural preservation.}. % at $l$-th layer
% where $\bm{Z}$ denotes the feature matrix of the external knowledge triple at the current $l$-th layer's input, composed of sequential feature vectors $[\bm{z}_1,..., \bm{z}_m,..., \bm{z}_M]$, where $\bm{z}_m$ corresponds to the $m$-th token in the knowledge triple sequence, and $M$ indicates the total token count in the current triple $Z$. 
% $\bm{Q}^Z = [q^Z_1,..., q^Z_m,..., q^Z_M]$, $\bm{K}^Z = [k^Z_1,..., k^Z_m,..., k^Z_M]$ and $\bm{V}^Z = [v^Z_1,..., v^Z_m,..., v^Z_M]$ represent the query, key and value matrices of the given knowledge triple, respectively. 
% the derived $(\bm{q}^Z_m, \bm{k}^Z_m, \bm{v}^Z_m)$ respectively represent the query, key and value features of the $m$-th token. 
% $\bm{W}^Q$, $\bm{W}^K$ and $\bm{W}^V$ are the weight matrices in self-attention at $l$-th layer\footnote{We directly reuse the original weights at each layer to ensure feature space consistency.}. 

After obtaining the triple representations, the \textbf{outward aggregation} flow is then formulated as:
% \begin{equation}
%     \hat{\bm{x}}_n = \frac{
%     \overbrace{\sum^{n}_{i=1} \text{Exp}((\bm{q}^x_n)^{\top} \bm{k}^X_i) \bm{v}^X_i}^{\text{\textit{aggregation on inputs: X}}} + 
%     \overbrace{\sum^{M}_{j=1} \text{Exp}((\bm{q}^x_n)^{\top} \bm{k}^Z_j) \bm{v}^Z_j}^{\text{\textit{aggregation on external KG: Z}}}
%     }{
%     \sum^{n}_{i=1} \text{Exp}((\bm{q}^x_n)^{\top} \bm{k}^X_i) + 
%     \sum^{M}_{j=1} \text{Exp}((\bm{q}^x_n)^{\top} \bm{k}^Z_j)
%     }
% \label{eq:stream2}
% \end{equation}
%
%
\begin{equation}
    \hat{\bm{x}}_n = \bigg\{
    \overbrace{\sum^{n}_{i=1} \text{Exp}(w^X_{n,i}) \bm{v}^X_i}^{\text{\textit{aggregation on inputs: X}}} + 
    \overbrace{\sum^{M}_{j=1} \text{Exp}(\frac{(\bm{q}^X_n)^{\top} \bm{k}^Z_j}{\sqrt{D}}) \bm{v}^Z_j}^{\text{\textit{aggregation on external Z via X}}}
    \bigg\}/\bigg\{
    \overbrace{\sum^{n}_{i=1} \text{Exp}(w^X_{n,i}) + 
    \sum^{M}_{j=1} \text{Exp}(\frac{(\bm{q}^X_n)^{\top} \bm{k}^Z_j}{\sqrt{D}})}^{\text{\textit{normalization}}}
    \bigg\}
\label{eq:stream2}
\end{equation}
where $w^X_{n,i} = \{(\bm{q}^X_n)^{\top} \bm{k}^X_i\}/\sqrt{D}$ is the original attention score of input to itself. 
$\bm{q}^X_n \in \bm{Q}^X$ (distinct from the triple query feature $\bm{q}^Z_m$) denotes the query vector of the $n$-th input token, with $\bm{k}_n^X \in \bm{K}^X$ and $\bm{v}_n^X \in \bm{V}^X$ representing the corresponding key and value vectors. 


% This aggregation fundamentally differs from the conventional cross-attention due to its critical considerations: (1) \textbf{preservation of input self-attention} retains the original input-to-input attention flow (first term in Eq.~\ref{eq:stream2}). 
%
% This aggregation fundamentally differs from the conventional cross-attention which does not perform the information aggregation of the input (\ie the first term in Eq.~\ref{eq:stream2}). 
% This attention-level interaction enables dynamic knowledge integration from KG to input sequence by simply changing the input triple string. 
% This enables our model to conduct the \textbf{dynamic fusion} of external knowledge very effectively, ensuring the adaptability of our method.
%
This outward aggregation enables input representations to actively ``aggregate'' information from external knowledge by the simple attention-level interaction, without any parameter updates. 
The pathway brings three key advantages: contextual adaptability (knowledge influence dynamically adjusts to input semantics), architectural purity (no interference with existing model architecture), and computational efficiency (linear scaling with triple length $M$). 
This fusion operates systematically across all transformer layers, exhibiting hierarchical specialization, \ie lexical-level fusion in lower layers, and semantic-level integration in higher layers. % (\eg entity linking between text and KG tokens), (\eg relation reasoning across fused representations)
%
% This fusion is systematically performed at each hidden layer through KGA's outward aggregation, establishing continuous knowledge interaction throughout the LLM hierarchy (\ie the aggregation at the lexical level of the low-level layers, and the semantic level of the high-level layers in LLMs). 

% \textcolor{blue}{Outward Aggregation}
% \textcolor{blue}{Exploration Flow‌}

% \subsection{Structured Re-Aggregation of Input Information}
\subsection{KG\texorpdfstring{$\to$}{lambda}Input (Inward) Aggregation: Structured Input Recalibration}\label{sec:flow2}
Building on the previous aggregation, we could achieve effective knowledge fusion. 
However, a key challenge lies in selecting relevant triples from $\mathcal{G}$ to avoid exhaustive computation over the entire knowledge graph. 
To address this, we introduce a complementary aggregation flow. 
This pathway complements the outward aggregation by first carrying out a knowledge graph-guided refinement of input representations. 
This could strategically suppress irrelevant signals with amplifying knowledge-critical patterns in the input sequence, effectively addressing the potential attention dispersion noise amplification issue in conventional self-attention \cite{ahmed2025mateiclmitigatingattentiondispersion,ye2025differential}. 
The core interaction is formally defined as: 
% While the previous section describes external knowledge fusion through input-driven KG aggregation, this complementary pathway in this section enables knowledge-guided refinement of input representations. 
% The inward aggregation mechanism leverages KG embeddings to filter task-irrelevant signals and enhance knowledge-critical patterns in the input sequence, effectively addressing \textit{the inherent noise amplification issue in conventional self-attention}. 
% This interaction is formally defined as:
\begin{equation}
    \bm{r}_m = \bigg\{
    \overbrace{\sum^{N}_{i=1} \text{Exp}(\frac{(\bm{q}^Z_m)^{\top} \bm{k}^X_i}{\sqrt{D}}) \bm{v}^X_i}^{\text{\textit{aggregation on input X by Z}}}
    \bigg\}/\bigg\{
    \overbrace{\sum^{N}_{i=1} \text{Exp}(\frac{(\bm{q}^Z_m)^{\top} \bm{k}^X_i}{\sqrt{D}})}^{\text{\textit{normalization}}}
    \bigg\}
\label{eq:stream3}
\end{equation}
where $\bm{r}_m$ denotes the recalibrated representation vector obtained by aggregating input representations $\bm{X}$ under the guidance of the $m$-th KG triple token $\bm{z}_m$. 
This vector represents the remaining information after carefully filtering the input information using $\bm{z}_m$. 
Crucially, this non-causal attention mechanism allows full input context visibility (unrestricted by causal masking), ensuring comprehensive contextual utilization during recalibration. 
The restructured input matrix $\bm{R} = \{ \bm{r}_1,..., \bm{r}_m,..., \bm{r}_M\}$ encodes KG-refined input representations across all $M$ triple tokens. 


\subsubsubsection{\textbf{Adaptive Consolidation}} After obtaining the recalibrated token-level representations, we can sum these feature vectors (\ie \{$\bm{r}_1$...$\bm{r}_m$\}) to obtain the input-level feature which is an aggregated input representation based on the entire triple. 
However, the importance of each token in the triple is not the same, which means that the importance of $\bm{r}_m$ should not be treated as the same. 
% If an uniform summation is performed, the important information may not be highlighted. 
If a uniform summation is applied, the importance of individual components may be diluted, potentially obscuring critical information. 
As such, we propose an attention-aware fusion strategy: 
\begin{equation}
    \hat{\bm{r}} = \bm{w}^{Z}_{M} \bm{R} = \sum\nolimits_{j=1}^M w^Z_{M,j} \bm{r}_j
\label{eq:summarization}
\end{equation}
Here, $w^Z_{M,j}$ represents the causal attention score between the $M$-th triple token (the last one) and the $j$-th token in $Z$, derived from the KG triple's native self-attention. 
% This design injects the model's inherent knowledge about triple token importance while maintaining architectural consistency. 
This design leverages the LLMs' inherent knowledge of the triple token importance, while preserving architectural consistency.
% This design: (1) preserves architectural consistency by reusing existing attention parameters
% (2) prioritizes structurally significant triple elements (\eg relation predicates) (3) maintains computational efficiency through weight inheritance. 

\subsubsubsection{\textbf{Triple Selection}}
% The consolidated input representation $\hat{\bm{r}}$ derived from Eq.~\ref{eq:summarization} enables systematic evaluation of input triple importance, thereby guiding knowledge triple selection in the initial outward aggregation phase and establishing a self-improving feedback loop to refine knowledge fusion dynamics. 
% Specifically, the refined representation interacts with the outward aggregation output through inner product scoring: 
The consolidated input representation $\hat{\bm{r}}$ derived from Eq.~\ref{eq:summarization} enables systematic evaluation of input triple importance, achieving a self-refining feedback mechanism. 
This process guides knowledge triple selection in the outward aggregation phase, optimizing the overall knowledge fusion dynamics. 
Formally, we compute relevance between the triple and input as: 
\begin{equation}
    s(Z, X) = \hat{\bm{r}}^\top \hat{\bm{x}_N}
\label{eq:importance}
\end{equation}
This similarity score quantifies the triple's contextual relevance to the input, enabling dynamic triple selection via top-k ranking. 
% The gating mechanism ensures that only knowledge-critical triples influence final predictions, effectively reducing computational overhead and noise propagation. 
% The core innovation is Semantic Refinement via Knowledge-Centric Reweighting; KG-Guided Attention over Input Tokens. 
This gating mechanism ensures knowledge-critical filtering, \ie only triples with high contextual alignment influence final predictions. 
% This could reduce computational overhead and noise propagation.

\subsection{Discussion}
Section~\ref{sec:flow1} delineates the external knowledge enhancement mechanism through input-driven triple integration (\ie outward aggregation). 
While this pathway shares superficial similarities with several conventional approaches, our framework exhibits fundamental architectural innovations. % as visually contrasted in Figure~\ref{fig:demo}. 
As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:kga-demo}, the proposed outward aggregation systematically integrates three essential fusion dimensions: (1) Triple-to-Input: Knowledge infusion from KG to input sequence, (2) Triple-Itself: Intra-token self-attention for semantic consolidation in a given triple (3) Input-Itself: Native self-attention for contextual coherence maintenance. 
This tripartite architecture enables simultaneous refinement of both input representations and knowledge embeddings through their intrinsic patterns. 
% Crucially, the Triple-to-Triple and Input-to-Input aggregations preserve critical intra-modality relationships that are often neglected in alternative approaches. 

However, \textbf{In-Context Learning} in Figure~\ref{fig:icl-demo} introduces uncontrolled inter-triple interference due to concatenating all triples as extended input. 
% 通过层数的不断叠加，从别的triple中聚合来的信息带来的影响可能会被放大
This forced co-processing of potentially unrelated triples (a) induces interference of different triples, (b) introduces sensitivity to triple ordering, and (c) unnecessary computation of inter-triple interaction and decreases the model efficiency. 
\textbf{Cross-Attention} in Figure~\ref{fig:cross-demo} restricts to unidirectional knowledge fusion (Triple$\to$Input) while failing to preserve essential attention flows of the input itself (\ie the first term in Eq.~\ref{eq:stream2}). 
This architectural deficiency prevents effective knowledge refinement (no Triple-Itself) and degrades input contextualization (without Input-Itself). 
% Our experiments (Section 5.3) quantitatively validate that the proposed tri-flow aggregation achieves 23.6\% higher knowledge utilization efficiency compared to these baselines, while maintaining comparable inference latency to standard self-attention implementations.



\input{4_experiments}





\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
This paper introduced a novel test-time knowledge fusion framework that dynamically integrates external knowledge graphs into large language models through parameter-preserving attention rewiring, eliminating the need for fine-tuning or architectural modifications. 
By establishing bidirectional interactions between textual inputs and triple tokens via outward and inward aggregation pathways, our method achieved competitive performance across knowledge-intensive tasks while maintaining the base model's general capabilities and computational efficiency. 
Experimental validation demonstrated its effectiveness, positioning the framework as a practical solution for deploying reliable, knowledge-aware LLMs in real-world scenarios. 
The interpretable attention patterns and modular design further enable seamless integration with evolving KGs, bridging the gap between parametric knowledge and symbolic reasoning without compromising deployment scalability.

\section{Limitation and Future Work}\label{sec:limitation}
Considering the feature space alignment, our current framework effectively reuses the original attention weights ($\bm{W}^Q/\bm{W}^K/\bm{W}^V$) for triple feature transformation (as elaborated in Section~\ref{sec:flow1}). 
However, it does not explicitly model structural information inherent in knowledge graphs. 
We are actively exploring integration with knowledge graph embedding (KGE) techniques through learnable transformation matrices that encode structural patterns (\eg relation hierarchies and graph connectivity). 
Preliminary investigations suggest that augmenting the parameter-sharing mechanism with lightweight structural adapters could enhance structure-aware representation learning while maintaining parameter efficiency. 
This direction may bridge the gap between discrete graph semantics and continuous language model representations, potentially improving performance on compositional reasoning tasks.

title: On the dimension of the solution space of linear difference equations over the ring of infinite sequences
summary:
For a linear difference equation with the coefficients being computable
sequences, we establish algorithmic undecidability of the problem of
determining the dimension of the solution space including the case when some
additional prior information on the dimension is available.

title: Towards Collaborative Fairness in Federated Learning Under Imbalanced Covariate Shift
summary:
Collaborative fairness is a crucial challenge in federated learning. However,
existing approaches often overlook a practical yet complex form of
heterogeneity: imbalanced covariate shift. We provide a theoretical analysis of
this setting, which motivates the design of FedAKD (Federated Asynchronous
Knowledge Distillation)- simple yet effective approach that balances accurate
prediction with collaborative fairness. FedAKD consists of client and server
updates. In the client update, we introduce a novel asynchronous knowledge
distillation strategy based on our preliminary analysis, which reveals that
while correctly predicted samples exhibit similar feature distributions across
clients, incorrectly predicted samples show significant variability. This
suggests that imbalanced covariate shift primarily arises from misclassified
samples. Leveraging this insight, our approach first applies traditional
knowledge distillation to update client models while keeping the global model
fixed. Next, we select correctly predicted high-confidence samples and update
the global model using these samples while keeping client models fixed. The
server update simply aggregates all client models. We further provide a
theoretical proof of FedAKD's convergence. Experimental results on public
datasets (FashionMNIST and CIFAR10) and a real-world Electronic Health Records
(EHR) dataset demonstrate that FedAKD significantly improves collaborative
fairness, enhances predictive accuracy, and fosters client participation even
under highly heterogeneous data distributions.

title: Virtuoso: High Resource Utilization and μs-scale Performance Isolation in a Shared Virtual Machine TCP Network Stack
summary:
Virtualization improves resource efficiency and ensures security and
performance isolation for cloud applications. Today, operators use a layered
architecture with separate network stack instances in each VM and container
connected to a virtual switch. Decoupling through layering reduces complexity,
but induces performance and resource overheads at odds with increasing demands
for network bandwidth, connection scalability, and low latency.
  We present Virtuoso, a new software network stack for VMs and containers.
Virtuoso re-organizes the network stack to maximize CPU utilization, enforce
isolation, and minimize processing overheads. We maximize utilization by
running one elastically shared network stack instance on dedicated cores; we
enforce isolation by performing central and fine-grained per-packet resource
accounting and scheduling; we reduce overheads by building a single-layer data
path with a one-shot fast-path incorporating all processing from the TCP
transport layer through network virtualization and virtual switching. Virtuoso
improves resource efficiency by up to 82%, latencies by up to 58% compared to
other virtualized network stacks without sacrificing isolation, and keeps
processing overhead within 6.7% of unvirtualized stacks.

\begin{abstract}
  Virtualization improves resource efficiency
  and ensures security and performance isolation
  for cloud applications. Today, operators
  use a layered architecture with
  separate network stack instances in each VM
  and container connected to a virtual switch.
  Decoupling through layering reduces
  complexity, but induces performance and resource
  overheads at odds with increasing demands
  for network bandwidth,
  connection scalability,
  %
  and low latency.

  We present \sys, a new software network stack for
  VMs and containers. \sys re-organizes the
  network stack to maximize CPU utilization and
  minimize processing overheads while enforcing isolation.
  We maximize
  utilization by running one elastically shared network stack instance
  on dedicated cores;
  we enforce isolation by performing
  central and fine-grained per-packet resource accounting
  and scheduling;
  we reduce overheads by building a single-layer data
  path with a one-shot fast-path incorporating all processing from
  the TCP transport layer through network virtualization and virtual
  switching.
  \sys improves resource efficiency by up to 82\%,
  latencies by up to 58\% compared to other virtualized network stacks
  without sacrificing isolation, achieving processing overhead within
  6.7\% of bare-metal stacks.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

The cloud leverages virtualization to improve resource utilization
while ensuring isolation for security and performance.
%
%
%
The hypervisor and operating system allocate and manage the shared
physical resources such as processor cores, memory, and network
links.
For network communication, each VM and container runs a separate
network stack instance.
%
VMs send packets from their OS stack through virtual NICs to the
hypervisor, while containers run in isolated network name spaces also
generating raw guest network packets, then forwarded through a virtual
interface to a central kernel or userspace virtual bridge or switch.
The operator configures the virtual switch to implement
network virtualization, including tunneling, bandwidth limits,
and security checks, and pass packets to and from the physical
network.

In this layered architecture, packets pass through a series of
separate loosely-coupled components, such as the guest transport
layer, network layer, virtual NIC and virtual switch.
%
This architecture simplifies development and management as
well as enabling some performance isolation with separate network
stacks for each guest.
However, this approach incurs substantial CPU and latency overheads,
especially for modern cloud applications requiring $\mu$s-scale
latencies~\cite{zhang:demikernel} while operating at bandwidths of up
to $400\,Gbps$.
Layered network processing incurs substantial overhead as some
processing steps, such as header accesses and state lookups, repeat
across components and access multiple different data
structures~\cite{kaufmann:tas,shashidhara:flextoe}.
The hypervisor individually mediates every packet sent or received by
the guest, increasing CPU overhead and communication latency.

%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
In this paper, we additionally argue that the existing layered virtual network
stack architecture sacrifices resource efficiency for isolation.
The typical static CPU allocation for guests (VMs or containers) requires
users to provision cores for peak traffic.
For communication-intensive applications a substantial fraction of
this peak CPU resources,
e.g. up to 48\% of cycles for a key-value store
~\cite{kaufmann:tas,shashidhara:flextoe},
are required for network processing.
However, the more common off-peak periods incur poor
CPU utilization because of idle capacity allocated for network
processing.
For instance, 84\% of VMs
have a peak utilization of less than 20\%~\cite{ghosh:bitingoff}.
%
%
Techniques, such as CPU oversubscription, can improve utilization
but are uncommon in clouds because of the difficulties
in maintaining tenant SLOs and performance isolation.
%
%
%
%


We argue that these performance and efficiency overheads are not
inherent to network virtualization, but are an artifact of the
existing architecture.
To that end, we propose a fundamental re-organization of the
full virtual network stack architecture, by combining three key ideas.
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
First, \sys uses only \emph{one network stack
instance} in the hypervisor, \emph{shared} by all guests.
%
%
%
Sharing improves CPU utilization for bursty workloads, as the shared
stack elastically allocates CPU resources just-in-time, rather than
statically provisioning CPU bandwidth for each guest's peak.
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
Second, to provide microsecond-scale performance isolation in a shared network
stack, we leverage \emph{fine-grained per-packet resource scheduling}.
\sys accounts CPU cycles and network bandwidth used for each processed
packet to the respective guest resource budget, scheduling each
guest on a per-packet basis. These fine-grained mechanisms incur minimal
performance overhead but enable $\mu$s-scale performance isolation.
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
Finally, a \emph{coalesced data path} combines all virtual network
processing from transport down to virtual switching. The coalesced
data path in \sys collapses all layers in the stack, minimizing
processing overheads by avoiding intermediate queuing, while
implementing the same functionality as conventional layered stacks,
with considerably fewer processor cycles.
We further split
the data path into a \emph{fast-} and a \emph{slow-path}. \sys
processes common packets for established connections on the fast-path
in \emph{one-shot}, reducing necessary state and simplifying
performance isolation through short, predictable code paths. Uncommon
cases are handled on the slow-path at a small performance penalty.
%
%
%
%


We present \sys, a new, shared software network stack for virtual
machines and containers that maximizes CPU utilization, while
minimizing processing overheads and enforcing isolation.
\sys is drop-in compatible with sockets and
TCP. It is optimized for latency-sensitive small packet communication
that is the common case behaviour for datacentre applications and
services~\cite{seemakhupt:rpc-charac}.
%
With its stack re-design, \sys improves resource
utilization by sharing the stack, while providing fine-grained
per-packet CPU performance isolation.
\sys improves resource efficiency by up to 82\% and increases
throughput by up to 91\% over optimized layered stacks, while still
ensuring $\mu$s-scale tail latency performance isolation.  \sys
also
achieves high absolute throughput, incurring only a 14\% throughput
penalty compared to state-of-the-art bare-metal network stacks.
Additionally, \sys helps improve the performance of small VMs
(VMs that are not even allocated a full core)
by reducing VM exits, thus providing opportunities
for cloud providers to improve networking performance on oversubscribed
machines.



\medskip
\noindent
Our contributions are the following:
\begin{compactitem}[\labelitemi]
\item The design of a new shared TCP network stack for virtual
  environments that improves resource utilization and leverages
  fine-grained scheduling for isolation.
\item One-shot network virtualization fast-path incurring minimal
  virtualization overhead.
\item \sys prototype implementation for Linux and QEMU.
\item Performance analysis of \sys prototype to quantify the resource
  utilization improvement and overhead reduction, and confirming
  performance isolation and low tail latency.
\end{compactitem}

\medskip
\noindent
We will release \sys as open-source software.
 %
\section{Background}%
%
\label{sec:bg}
We now discuss the unique challenges for and approaches to network
communication in virtualized environments.
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%

\subsection{Network Virtualization Concepts}
\label{subsec:bg-netvirt}
Virtualization aims to facilitate management and consolidation of
physical resources.
Multiple guest VMs or containers with separate network addresses share
a single physical host, network controller, and link.
Similarly, multiple separate virtual networks share the same physical
network.
%
%
%
Tenants expect to flexibly configure and use their virtual
infrastructure and
operators must multiplex the physical resources
providing isolation to produce the illusion of completely separate
infrastructure to mutually non-trusting tenants.

%
%
%
%
%
%

On the hosts this requires virtual switching, moving packets between
guests and the shared physical network in a controlled and
safe way, and enforcing all necessary processing for security and
isolation.
In the network, virtualization requires
tunneling~\cite{rfc:vxlan, rfc:nvgre, rfc:geneve}
to encapsulate packets, enabling use of
separate protocols and routing on the physical network.
Virtual switching also assigns appropriate physical network addresses
based on virtual network addresses.

The complete network communication infrastructure aims to meet the
following \emph{operator goals}: guests must not affect the performance
of other guests, idle resources should be minimized, and packets
must not be tampered with. In addition,
there are two \emph{tenant goals}: the networking stack
must support $\mu$s scale latencies and high throughput.

%
%
%
%

%
%
%
%
%

%
%
%
%

%
%
%
%
%
%

%
%
%
%

\subsection{Status Quo: Layered Silos}
\label{subsec:bg-indep-stacks}
Traditionally, network virtualization is implemented as a deeply
layered architecture (\autoref{fig:trad-arch}). Packet processing is
divided between independent network stacks in each guest (managed by the
tenant), multiplexed by the virtual switch running as the lowest layer
on the host (managed by the operator).  Guests send and receive raw
network packets through their conventional OS network stack via the
assigned virtual NIC (vNIC) just as in a native deployment.
Containers run in separate network namespaces typically communicating
with the outside through \texttt{veth} pairs~\cite{spec:veth}, while VMs
run separate OS instances and use vNICs such as
\texttt{virtio-net}~\cite{spec:virtio} implemented by the hypervisor.

The virtual switch (vSwitch) takes packets sent on the guests' vNICs,
routes and encapsulates them for the physical network, and then sends
them out through the host's physical NIC. Receiving packets works
symmetrically: packets arrive on the physical NIC, the vSwitch
inspects and decapsulates them to determine the virtual network, and
then looks up and passes them to the corresponding vNIC.
%
%
%
%
Alternatively, some deployments
leverage hardware SR-IOV~\cite{spec:intel_sriov}
capabilities to bypass the software switch
layer of the virtualization stack and increase performance,
by assigning resources on the NIC to the guest through \emph{virtual
  functions} (VFs).
%

\paragraph{Advantages.}
Separately developed, maintained, and operated virtual switches
simplify implementation and enable flexible deployment.
Typically data centers run guest VMs and containers on dedicated
cores.
Thus, independent per-guest stacks effectively silo applications,
reducing fate-sharing and minimizing inter-VM performance interference.
%
%
Much of the protocol processing happens in the guest and is thus
automatically accounted for and isolated.
Early demultiplexing can also aid to prevent priority inversion, as packet
priorities are only known afterwards~\cite{mosberger:scout}.

\paragraph{Disadvantages.}
Layered network stacks incur overheads increasing latency and
wasting CPU
cycles~\cite{kaufmann:tas,peter:arrakis}.
Each layer adds indirection, through queues or other communication mechanisms.
For example, the TCP layer generates segments that queue
lower in the stack because of vSwitch-enforced bandwidth limits.
Further, independent layers often redundantly retrieve packet
information from different data structures~\cite{mosberger:scout}.
%
%
Layered stacks also include significant processing before
multiplexing points that are not performance isolated, e.g. in the
vSwitch.
This is a source of performance cross-talk between guests, increasing tail
latency~\cite{tennenhouse:layered_multiplexing}.

Siloed network stacks further require over-provisioning of
resources.
For the typically bursty workloads, tenants have to provision VMs with
enough resources (especially cores) for peak bandwidth\cite{reidys:coach}.
While VMs can share resources such as CPU cores, this is not
compatible with $\mu$s-scale latency requirements because of
long and expensive VM context switches.
Cloud VMs, in particular, typically exclusively provision processor
cores. The only exceptions are the smallest and cheapest instance
types.
VMs rarely operate at peak traffic, frequently
leaving resources underutilized.

\paragraph{SR-IOV is not a panacea.}
SR-IOV bypasses virtualization layers and reduces overhead,
but it also comes with drawbacks. Namely, SR-IOV is not compatible
with every network adapter and can lead to underutilized resources
because NIC resources are assigned to specific VMs.
For example, the network virtualization stack for Google Cloud skirts
SR-IOV so that guests do not have to cope with different physical
NIC resources on the target host during live migration~\cite{dalton:andromeda}.
SR-IOV also only allows NIC resources to be multiplexed,
but not the cores used by a VM's network stack for packet
processing, thus forgoing sharing opportunities.

\paragraph{Summary.}
\label{subsec:bg-challenges}
Siloed stacks face two key challenges.
First, there is a \emph{trade-off between isolation and resource
utilization}.
Multiplexing resources early with independent stacks facilitates
isolation but fails to capitalize on finer-grained resource-sharing
opportunities because resources are siloed from the start and cannot
be pooled at lower levels.
Second, \emph{layering provides modularity but leads to
overheads} in packet processing. These overheads are
exacerbated by rising network speeds, $\mu$s tail-latency
requirements~\cite{dean:tail_atscale}, and the large scale of
datacenter applications. A shared network stack exposed with
application interfaces as the abstraction boundary instead of a virtual NIC
can improve utilization
and allows rapid and flexible deployment, thus accelerating innovation
in the cloud~\cite{niu:netstackservice}. Performance isolation can
be implemented as part of the shared stack to prevent VM interference.
Backward compatibility and integration with existing systems is a concern
with shared stacks, but features such as access control and
network policies can be integrated as part of the shared stack and enforced
at connection time by integrating the shared stack with other existing
technologies such as OvS~\cite{software:ovs}. Shared stacks present
challenges, but provide benefits to modern clouds compared to siloed stacks.

\subsection{Prior Work}
\label{subsec:bg-non-solutions}
Prior work has investigated these challenges, but fails to satisfy all
goals. In particular, providing high resource utilization and CPU elasticity
with minimal interference for $\mu$s-scale workloads
remains a challenge.

\paragraph{Reducing layering overheads.}
A range of work avoids layering overheads and reduces
indirection in packet processing in specific layers. These
solutions span kernel bypass~\cite{belay:ix,
jeong:mtcp, zhang:demikernel, peter:arrakis, druschel:osiris},
kernel offload via eBPF~\cite{ghigoff:bmc, zhou:electrode, qi:spright},
zero-copy methods~\cite{chu:solaris, peter:arrakis, belay:ix, li:socksdirect},
new NIC interfaces~\cite{sadok:enso,pismenny:shring,
voneicken:unet,eran:nica},
and one-shot unlayered
fast-paths~\cite{kaufmann:tas,shashidhara:flextoe}. These approaches
do not completely solve performance overheads or isolation across the
virtualized stack. They instead focus on streamlining the
path between application and NIC by reducing operating system
overheads, but neglect the additional layers necessary for network
virtualization, or suffer from low utilization and isolation
as they lack elasticity and performance isolation mechanisms.

\paragraph{Hardware offload.}
Offloading parts of network virtualization processing can
significantly reduce overheads. Recent data center NICs support
offload for VXLAN, GENEVE, and NVGRE~\cite{spec:mellanox_connectx7}
en/de-capsulation.
Complete offload of virtual switching
fast-paths~\cite{firestone:vfp,luo:vswitchoffload,spec:nvidia_bluefield3},
and hypervisor bypass~\cite{product:amazon:nitro, product:microsoft:catapult},
can reduce
overheads
further and enable direct HW NIC access for guests through
SR-IOV~\cite{firestone:vfp,product:amazon:nitro}.  However, these
approaches rely on fixed hardware limited to specific
protocols and features~\cite{firestone:vfp}, or themselves leverage
multi-core
SmartNICs~\cite{product:amazon:nitro,luo:vswitchoffload,spec:nvidia_bluefield3}
and FPGAs~\cite{product:microsoft:catapult},
resulting in another layered architecture with the challenges
above. Hardware offload also gives rise to other
performance isolation challenges with shared hardware resources, such
as the NIC, PCIe interconnect, and IOMMU~\cite{agarwal:hi_congestion}.
Finally, software solutions remain relevant because of their comparative
flexibility and simple deployability as evidenced by software networking
stacks deployed large-scale in production~\cite{marty:snap,dalton:andromeda,kumar:picnic}.

\section{\sys Approach}%
\label{sec:principles}

%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%

%

\centering%

\caption{Fast-path manages TX and RX;

\label{fig:sys-arch}%

%


\sys (\autoref{fig:sys-arch}) eliminates the tradeoff between resource
efficiency and isolation by sharing a network stack among guests and
implementing
isolation in a single layer.
The shared stack allows \sys to elastically pool resources and increase utilization,
while fine-grained resource accounting and scheduling ensure performance
isolation. Externalizing network processing gives \sys visibility into
VM usage, so that it can make informed scheduling decisions about
multiple VMs.
%
\sys uses a multi-threaded data fast-path with dedicated cores for
common case send and receive operations, and a separate slow-path for
data path exceptions and control operations.  The fast-path combines
all network virtualization and packet processing layers up to and
including the TCP transport layer, minimizing the path between the
guest application and the host NIC. The small units of work in the
fast-path enable \sys to perform fine-grained per packet scheduling
efficiently.
The fast-path implements
en-/de-capsulation and de-multiplexing, and combines all common-case
processing. Only the sockets interface remains in the guest, but is
tightly integrated with guest applications in guest userspace through
a dynamic link library.

\subsection{Design Principles}

\paragraph{Shared network stack for elastic resource utilization.}
Instead of partitioning network processing to multiple guest silos and
the hypervisor, \sys places one shared network stack instance in the
hypervisor.  Externalizing network processing allows guests to serve
the same workload with fewer cores; we instead re-allocate some of
these cores for the shared stack.  This resource consolidation
particularly improves utilization for bursty workloads by being
elastic; the larger shared pool of cores can absorb bursts better than
multiple static per-guest pools~\cite{wischik:pooling_principle}.
Furthermore, a shared network stack also improves deployment flexibility
and allows providers to offer more meaningful SLAs to tenants by taking
control over the stack~\cite{niu:netstackservice}.

\paragraph{Fine-grained per-packet scheduling for isolation.}
Instead of coarse-grained resource management via dedicated
cores to guests, we employ central and fine-grained resource accounting and
scheduling for individual packets to ensure isolation in the
shared network stack. \sys precisely accounts processor cycles and
network bandwidth spent by each packet to the respective
guest resource budget. \sys leverages global visibility across all
guests combined with accurate resource accounting to implement
fine-grained per-packet scheduling that enforces tight isolation policies.
Scheduling is implemented
centrally at a single layer in the system, minimizing
crosstalk~\cite{tennenhouse:layered_multiplexing, leslie:nemesis}.
This nimble mechanism incurs minimal performance overhead but enables
performance isolation even for microsecond-scale latencies.
%

\paragraph{Single-layer data path.}
%
Instead of layered processing, \sys leverages a single-layer data
path, coalescing all network processing from the TCP transport layer
down to network virtualization and virtual switching, for receive and
transmit. Guest applications interact directly with the data path
through efficient shared memory queues, by linking a dynamic link
library in guest userspace that provides the TCP sockets API. This
allows \sys to implement the same functionality as conventional
layered stacks considerably faster and with fewer processor cycles by
communicating directly with the single-layer data path.

\paragraph{One-shot fast-path.}
We further streamline the \sys data path via a one-shot fast-path. For
each TCP connection, \emph{one-shot processing} pre-computes rarely
changing processing state, such as guest and physical IP routing and
tunnel state, storing it in the fast-path, reducing per-packet
processing overhead for common packets of established
connections. Handling a limited number of common cases in the
fast-path also simplifies performance isolation through short and
predictable code paths.
%
%
%
For example, when sending a TCP segment from the guest on a virtual
TCP connection, the fast-path can directly create a physical packet with
all relevant virtualization headers and send it via the host NIC in a
short operation. Uncommon cases are handled on a separate slow-path at
a small performance penalty.

\section{Detailed \sys Design}%
\label{sec:design}

%
In \sys, a multi-core fast-path polls guests for new
packets and parses and generates headers in a single layer for
low-overhead packet transmission and reception.  The fast-path
accesses each guest library's shared memory region and aggregates
packets from multiple guests into a batch to increase utilization. A
separate slow-path core handles control operations and exceptions.
\sys moves congestion control updates (still enforced in fast-path),
connection control, timeouts, and error handling to the slow path.
Dividing tasks between a fast-path and a slow-path allows us to
reduce overheads by streamlining the fast-path.
%
%
For initialization of these shared memory channels between
applications and \sys during startup, we leverage a modified
hypervisor for guests and the host OS for containers.  We describe these
implementations later (\autoref{subsec:containers}, \autoref{subsec:ivshm}).
After shared memory regions are set up,
there are no differences for the application-\sys data path between
virtual machines and containers. Hence, we refer to them collectively
as \emph{guests}.

In this section, we describe the different \sys components.
%
We start by
describing how we integrate efficient network virtualization in a
multi-core fast-path (\autoref{subsec:network_virtualization}).
We then describe how we track each guest's resource usage on
individual fast-path cores through a per-guest budget
(\autoref{subsec:budgeting}), followed by a discussion of how we use
this information to coordinate guest resource budget allocation across
fast-path cores centrally through our slow-path
(\autoref{subsec:centralsched}).
We then describe our fine-grained scheduling based on the
per-guest resource budgets (\autoref{subsec:scheduling}).
Finally, we describe how we protect the \sys stack %
when sharing it among guests (\autoref{subsec:sharednetstack}).

\subsection{One-shot, Single-layer Transport}
\label{subsec:network_virtualization}

%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
\begin{figure}[t]%
\centering%
\includegraphics[width=0.47\textwidth]{figures/slow-fast-path.pdf}%
\caption{The fast path routes packets to VMs with cached state;
    the slow path fetches tunnel headers on cache misses.}%
\label{fig:slowfastpath}%
\end{figure}
%
\paragraph{Single-layer transport.}
\sys combines all
processing from the TCP transport layer all the way down to network
virtualization into a streamlined one-shot fast-path
(\autoref{fig:slowfastpath}), for send and receive.  Separating out
common case processing in a minimal fast-path enables
performance optimization, while a separate slow-path ensures that less
frequent cases are handled.  Regular data transfer packets
for established TCP connections exclusively use this optimized data
path, while packets for unknown connections or other protocols pass
through the slow-path.  The slow-path sets up one-shot fast-path
state for for new connections so
future packets remain on the fast-path (\autoref{fig:slowfastpath}).

%
On receive, the fast-path parses the packet according to the expected
format, configured by default to TCP over IPv4 on the guest side,
encapsulated in GRE~\cite{rfc:gre} over IPv4, and Ethernet on
the physical network.
The fast-path then leverages the corresponding connection identifiers,
TCP ports, guest IPs, and tunnel ID to look up the consolidated flow
state.
After validating the packet against the state, the fast-path directly
stores the TCP payload in the guest flow buffer and enqueues a
notification in the corresponding guest receive queue.
Finally, if necessary, we reformat the packet by swapping addresses
and tweaking the TCP header into a response TCP acknowledgement.

%
Similarly for transmit, once \sys schedules a flow to transmit a
packet, the flow state directly provides all necessary state to
directly assemble the complete packet with all headers for immediate
transmission via the NIC.
Headers are divided between inner and outer headers.
The inner TCP and IP headers includes the source and destination IP
address and port on the guest (virtual) network.
The outer headers include the GRE encapsulation with the key field to
identify the network~\cite{rfc:gre_extended} wrapped by the outer UDP
and IP header and corresponding physical network source and
destination IP addresses and ports, finally wrapped by Ethernet and
the necessary peer MAC address.
\sys stores these key fields in the consolidated flow state.

\paragraph{One-shot fast-path processing.}
We implement this processing as straight-line code with minimal
control flow (other than exceptions for rare cases) and no packet
modifications until acknowledgements~\cite{kaufmann:tas}.
\sys processes packet in one shot without intermediate queuing or
access to complex data structures other than the consolidated flow
state.
We skip some steps for conventional network virtualization such as
decapsulation completely.
Other steps we combine with already necessary related steps previously
in other layers, such as combining the virtual switching table lookup
with the TCP flow state lookup.

Our state consolidation optimizations rely on most of this
state, such as guest routing, tunneling, host addressing and routing,
remaining typically unchanged over the life of a connection.
Thus it can be pre-computed and stored when a new connection is established.
This is related to other fast-path caches for virtual switching state
in systems such as Open vSwitch~\cite{software:ovs}.
Except \sys explicitly and eagerly manages this state, adding it,
updating it, and removing it as necessary instead of relying on misses
and invalidations.
This also implies that changes to this state are more expensive in
\sys than in other systems, as many changes to individual connection
state instances on the fast-path may be required for an individual
change to the underlying state.

\paragraph{Slow-path for remaining processing.}
The \sys slow-path handles all packets not handled by the fast-path.
This includes packets that are not TCP data packets, TCP control
packets to open and close connections as well as non-TCP packets.
We leverage the existing Open vSwitch~\cite{software:ovs} in the
slow-path for network virtualization. \sys sends truncated headers
to OvS, which asynchronously sends back the packet with the
necessary virtualization state. If the packet belongs to a
new TCP connection, \sys combines the received virtualization
state with the necessary TCP state.
Non-TCP packets are forwarded to guests through legacy interfaces
(vNICs or veth) for processing in the legacy stack.

\subsection{CPU Resource Accounting}
\label{subsec:budgeting}

%
\paragraph{Core-local resource accounting.}
The first step towards isolation is to accurately account
resource use. Each fast-path core tracks resources available to
and used on behalf of individual guests through a local budget table, storing
each guest's resource budget on that core. The slow-path periodically
updates the fast-path value (\autoref{subsec:centralsched}) and
replenishes budgets by performing an atomic add to the guest's budget
table entry. This minimizes synchronization on the
fast-path and improves overall throughput by 4.3\% at scale.

%
%
%
%
%
%
\paragraph{Batch processing in three main tasks.}
The \sys fast-path performs three main CPU-intensive tasks for guests:
receiving packets (RX), polling guest transmit queues (POLL), and
packet transmission (TX).
RX dequeues incoming packets from the NIC, parses the packets, and
implements the necessary TCP processing before forwarding the payload
to the guest.
POLL checks outgoing queues from guest applications to the fast-path
for new transmission requests.
%
%
%
%
%
%
TX assembles complete network-virtualized TCP packets and enqueues
them in the NIC. For efficiency, these tasks execute in batches,
generally from multiple guests.
The batch size is a compile-time parameter and primarily depends on
the system's cache hierarchy; we chose 16 empirically as the value
that yielded the highest throughput for our setup.

\paragraph{Lightweight accounting with TSCs.}
\sys measures CPU consumption with the CPU time stamp counter (TSC)
at the start and end of processing for each batch. Reading
the TSC is lightweight and precise. \sys breaks down the TSC total
to separate guests, based on each guest's number of packets. As
per-packet processing costs are generally similar, this represents a
reasonable trade-off between accounting overhead and
accuracy, as we will show later (\autoref{subsec:perf_iso},
\autoref{subsec:virt_overheads}).
\sys then subtracts the cycles consumed from the respective guest's
resource budget.

%
A separate slow-path core periodically replenishes the per-core
budgets on the fast-path, leveraging its global view.
Separation into a parallel de-centralized fast-path and a central
slow-path enables scalable and efficient coordination of the
frequently accessed per-core budgets.
The slow-path replenishes the total budget in periodic 100 µs
intervals and %
%
distributes the new budget to each guest.
The distribution among guests is controlled by a guest weight $w_g$,
configured by the operator. By default each guest has the same weight.

%
We compute update credits $e_g$ for guest $g$ by recording the
timestamp $t^\prime$ for the current update and the timestamp $t$ for
the previous update.  The allocator scales the elapsed time
$t^\prime - t$ by a constant boost $B$.
$B$ compensates for any fast-path CPU cycles not explicitly accounted
to any guest by \sys to avoid over-committing processor cycles.
We found the fraction of accounted cycles to be 94\% (and set
$B=0.94$), with minimal processing not related to specific guests.
This includes functions, such as scaling fast-path cores up and down
and checking if a core can block.
%
%
%
We multiply the product of the boost and elapsed cycles by the
guests's $w_g$, divided by the sum of the weights of all $n$ guests.
%
\begin{equation}
  e_g = \frac{B (t^\prime - t) w_g}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_k}
  \label{eq:budget_increment}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Work-conserving allocator distributes more credits to active cores.}
Our schedulers are work-conserving, so credits are proportionately
distributed based on activity.
This prevents a VM from being throttled when it runs out of
budget in a core, but has spare credits in other cores.
For example, if a guest only
uses one fast-path core, our resource allocator redistributes
credits assigned to other cores in this round to the active core.
We redistribute credits by calculating the sum of the used budget
$(b_{max} - b_{gc})$
for all $m$ cores and calculate the ratio of a core's
unused budget to the total sum. We multiply $e_g$ by this ratio.
This compromise helps minimize synchronization overhead with
per-core budgets,
while leveraging a global view to update local cores
every 100 $\mu$:
%
\begin{equation}
 u_{gc} = \frac{e_{g} (b_{max} - b_{gc})}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}(b_{max} - b_{gj})}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Preventing guest from accumulating budget.}
The operator also configures a budget cap $C$ for all guests. This cap
prevents guests from accumulating arbitrary budgets during
low utilization periods and starving other guests with bursty
activity. $C$ restricts the number of CPU cycles \sys can
spend on behalf of a guest per fast-path core between update periods.
The slow-path calculates the updated per-core
budget $b^\prime_{gc} = \min{\{C, b_{gc} + u_g\}}$ for guest $g$ on core $c$%
%

%
%
%
%

\autoref{fig:sensitivity-cap-boost} shows how different boost, budget
cap, and update period parameters
protect the performance of a guest VM,
while an aggressor VM introduces performance interference
through background load. The aggressor creates a load imbalance
by using 9 cores to open a total of 900 connections and the victim
opens one connection in one core.
If the boost parameter is excessively high, the performance of the guest
is affected because the aggressor is not sufficiently throttled:
the aggressor budget is fully replenished to the capped amount every round.
Similarly, if it is too low, the victim suffers a small tail
latency increase due to throttling.
In the experiment varying the budget cap, the aggressor bursts
every 250 ms for 250 ms. For large budget caps, the aggresssor
affects the performance of the victim if it is allowed to
accumulate credits by remaining momentarily idle.
Finally, by varying the update period granularity
we show shorter update periods help maintain
low $\mu$s-scale tail-latencies.

\subsection{Fine-grained Scheduling}
\label{subsec:scheduling}

\begin{figure}[t]%
\centering%
\includegraphics[width=0.47\textwidth]{figures/budgeting.pdf}%
\caption{Fast-path cores utilize a guest's local budget for processing tasks;
    all tasks measure resource consumption,
    with the slow-path periodically replenishing budgets}%
\label{fig:budgeting}%
\end{figure}

\sys enforces performance isolation with fine-grained hierarchical
scheduling based on per-guest CPU cycle budgets
(\autoref{fig:budgeting}). \sys first chooses guests to perform
work for, and when sending packets determines which
of the guest's flows get to transmit next.
Before the fast-path starts a task on behalf of a guest, the core
consults the guest's budget, and
if insufficient moves on to a different guest.
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%

\paragraph{Bounded fast-path simplifies scheduling.}
The observation at the center of our approach is that all individually
scheduled tasks are strictly bounded, on the order of 200--500 cycles
depending on packet sizes.
This provides us with two key
advantages.  First, \emph{preemption is not necessary}, as individual
packet processing tasks complete very
quickly.
Second, \emph{fine-grained batch scheduling and accurate accounting
enable low tail latency and isolation}, even without knowing
concrete task lengths.  Tasks are all similarly sized, and, after each
task completes, the next scheduling decision can compensate based on
the updated budget.  Even if a task overruns the budget, it
will only be by a small amount of cycles and \sys still precisely
accounts for this with negative budgets, akin to deficit round-robin
scheduling~\cite{shreedhar:drr}.

These two observations enable fine-grained scheduling for low tail latency
without preemption overhead in \sys. Conventional layered network
stacks switch between guests and require context switches, which
disrupt CPU pipelines, cause cache overheads, and demand expensive
state saving and restoration~\cite{humphries:against_ctx_switches}.
\sys stores all necessary processing state in the corresponding
flow-state data structure, so
switching to processing a packet for a different guest
incurs minimal overhead, as it does not require any context switch.
%
%

\paragraph{Hierarchical scheduler controls guests and flows.}
\sys uses a two-level hierarchical scheduler.  The first level decides
which guest should be serviced next and the second level decides what
flow (TX) or transmit queue (POLL) from the selected guest should be
scheduled, using different policies.
This allows us to control resource allocation between
guests and between guest's flows and transmit queues. For RX,
\sys only performs resource accounting, as the specific guest is not
known before initial processing of the packets, preventing
scheduling. The following paragraphs dive into detail on scheduling
\sys processing tasks.

\paragraph{Batch-scheduling POLL}
\sys polls guest queues for new connection send
requests.  The fast-path polls each guest transmit queue in a batched
round-robin fashion to balance efficiency and low tail latency.
First, the fast-path core
selects the next guest and then starts polling the guest's transmit
queues, until the batch is full, all the guest's queues are empty,
or the guest resource budget is used up.  If the batch is not full,
the scheduler moves on to the next guest.
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%

%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%

Pulling multiple transmit requests from a queue in one batch
significantly reduces per-request overheads for queue access.
Consolidating tasks for a specific guest within a batch also increases
resource accounting accuracy as work from fewer guests is aggregated
in the same batch.  Even across guests, processing requests in
batches improves \sys efficiency by avoiding cache misses on
key memory accesses through group prefetching~\cite{kalia:gpupproc}.
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%
%

\paragraph{Scheduling TX for per-guest fairness.}
\sys also schedules transmit tasks with a similar batched hierarchical
approach (\autoref{alg:txscheduler}).  The scheduler first chooses the
next guest, and then the guest's next flow.
In the first level of the scheduler, round-robin determines the next
guest to send.  The second level schedules flows according to a priority
queue tracking the earliest time when each flow should send next.
The TCP processing logic determines these timestamps with a split
fast-path/slow-path congestion control scheme~\cite{kaufmann:tas}.
These timestamps also ensure that a guest's flows are
serviced fairly.
Guests without available budget are skipped until the budget is
replenished.

\begin{algorithm}[t]%
\caption{TX Scheduler}\label{alg:txscheduler}%
\begin{algorithmic}
  \Function{schedule\_vms}{vms}
    \State n $\gets$ batch\_size
    \For{vm in vms}
      \If{vm.budget > 0 and n > 0}
        \State n $\gets$ n - \Call{schedule\_flows}{vm.flows, n}
      \EndIf
    \EndFor
  \EndFunction

  \Function{schedule\_flows}{flows, n}
    \State i $\gets$ 0
    \For{f in flows}
      \If{i < n}
        \State i $\gets$ i + \Call{schedule\_packets}{f.packets, n - i}
      \EndIf
    \EndFor
  \EndFunction
\end{algorithmic}%
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Drop packets for out of budget VMs in RX.}
RX pulls packets from the NIC queues and performs
a flow state lookup to identify the destination VM of the packet.
\sys then drops the packet if it belongs to an out of budget VM.
This prevents a sender from overwhelming the receiver, causing the
receiving VM to use more than its fair share of resources.
We found that latency can
deteriorate by 2$\times$ when not dropping, but with drops, \sys ensures
performance isolation akin to siloed stacks
(\autoref{fig:perfiso}).
Per-VM hardware queues could attenuate packet drps drops, but the
larger number of queues incurs PCIe overhead~\cite{manesh:nic_queue_perf}.
Alternatively, systems such as
PicNIC~\cite{kumar:picnic} use per-VM software queues but cannot
prevent drops of excess traffic and wasted work.

The system is self-correcting when sender and receiver
enforce similar budget parameters,
\sys keeps track of the cycle deficit
accrued when later replenishing
the budget. Guests that deplete their budget on RX tasks as a result
have fewer cycles available for POLL and TX tasks, so senders that
do not receive replies will stop sending.

\paragraph{Round-robin packet scheduling on the slow-path.} The
slow-path employs per-VM packet queues and does round-robin scheduling
among these queues to prevent starvation. This avoids the
slow-path from harming the tail-latency of VMs when slow path requests are
skewed towards only a few VMs. For example, when the slow-path
congestion control algorithm calculates per-flow rates we have per-VM
flow queues, such that each VM is fairly serviced.

\subsection{Secure Shared Stack}
\label{subsec:sharednetstack}

\sys processes packets from multiple guests and applications in the
same network stack.  Resource accounting and scheduling mechanisms
provide performance isolation. For this we rely on shared memory
queues between individual application cores and the fast-path, as well
as a separate slow-path for more expensive control operations, akin to
TAS~\cite{kaufmann:tas} and SNAP~\cite{marty:snap}. However, we also
need security enforcement while enabling efficient direct
communication between applications and the \sys stack.

\paragraph{Protecting memory regions.}
\sys ensures security isolation for the guest and application
interface through memory isolation.  We allocate different guests'
queues and connection buffers in separate shared memory regions only
mapped into a single guest and the fast-path.  To avoid leaks due to
dynamic remapping and ensure resource isolation, \sys statically
pre-allocates the complete shared memory region when the guest starts.
\sys also has a narrow shared memory interface comprising
just guest receive and send queues along with connection payload
buffers.  This narrow interface provides no other attack
vectors, such as complex data structures that could interfere with
\sys.

\paragraph{Narrow interface reduces attack surface.}
\sys provides a simple interface to the guest OS using shared
memory queues, with only pre-defined memory regions from the \sys
stack mapped to guests. These regions contain only message passing queues
and connection buffers, with no memory shared among tenants. %
%
%
Similar to virtio-net~/cite{spec:virtio}, \sys identifies tenants
based on queues and uses corresponding data structures during
processing.

\section{Implementation}%
\label{sec:impl}
\sys runs in host userspace as a separate service and
provides all features of a typical TCP stack to guest applications.
\sys maintains TCP protocol and sockets API drop-in compatibility.
For fast NIC access, we use DPDK~\cite{software:dpdk}.
We build our prototype using TAS~\cite{kaufmann:tas} as a
basis.
We heavily modify and extend the TAS fast and slow-path, but retain
the sockets emulation library unmodified.
\sys supports guest VMs as well as guest containers.
The \sys prototype comprises 20,918 lines total, 4,669 lines for the
fast-path, 5,536 lines for the slow-path, 2,437 lines for the hypervisor
integration, and 1,029 lines of modification to OvS.

\subsection{Support for Multiple Guests}
%
%
We modify TAS to use separate shared memory regions on the host
and Unix sockets per guest.
These regions contain transmit request and receive notification
queues, as well as per-flow RX and TX circular payload buffers.
During guest initialization, \sys passes a newly created
shared memory region to the guest.
As in TAS we implement this using Unix domain sockets, that carry a
handshake along with the shared memory file descriptor.
Unlike TAS, \sys exposes separate listening Unix sockets for each
guest, allowing it to securely identify which guest is connecting,
assuming sufficient access control on the host.

\subsection{\sys with Containers}
\label{subsec:containers}
Given that guest containers share the same host operating system as
\sys, connecting applications in guest containers is simply a matter
of mapping the respective guest Unix socket into the container.
After this any container guest application can interact with \sys
as a native application with the same performance.

\subsection{\sys with Virtual Machines}
\label{subsec:ivshm}
Initialization is more complex for virtual machines, as Unix
sockets and file descriptors are by definition local to the host.
\sys instead integrates with the hypervisor to directly map shared
memory regions via a dummy PCI device.
In the VM, a \sys guest agent implements a user space driver for this
dummy device and translates the interface into a
compatible Unix socket and shared memory file descriptors,
avoiding the need for applications to distinguish between native,
container, and VM operation. No modifications are done to
the guest operating system.

We utilize QEMU~\cite{software:qemu} with KVM, along with its
Inter-VM Shared Memory Device (IVSHM)~\cite{software:ivshm},
to implement the hypervisor component of the \sys integration.
IVSHM allows an external application to send a shared memory
file descriptor and eventfds for bi-directional interrupts to QEMU
that are then exposed as a PCI device with the memory region as a
directly memory mapped BAR.
For ease of integration, we implement this as a separate host proxy
process that connects to QEMU and \sys.

In the guest we implement a \sys guest agent, that leverages the
vfio-pci~\cite{software:vfio-pci} kernel module to implement a user
space driver for the dummy PCI device.
vfio-pci provides a file descriptor that the application can mmap for
access to the BAR, along with eventfds for interrupts.
The guest agent creates a listening unix socket, and during the
handshake passes file descriptors directly to applications.
This results in a directly shared memory region between \sys on the
host, and applications in the guest VM.
As a result, fast-path interactions with \sys incur no additional
overheads compared to containers or native applications.

\subsection{OvS Slow-path}
\label{subsec:ovs}
We use OvS for virtualization management, to identify tunnelling
information, and to determine the destination VM for a flow.
To that end, we modify OvS to exchange packets and control information
with \sys.
In OvS we implement custom transmit and receive netdev-provider ports.
The receive port polls \sys for new packets and passes them to OvS.
OvS then performs internal matching based on the packet metadata and
directs it to a transmit netdev-provider port.
The transmit port holds tunnelling information for a packet and
establishes a message queue with \sys to dispatch this information.
This message queue exchanges inner and outer IP addresses for
encapsulated packets, tunnel IDs from GRE headers, and the appropriate
ID for the destination VM.

\section{Evaluation}%
\label{sec:eval}

In this section we evaluate how well \sys addresses the goals
outlined in \autoref{sec:bg} by answering the following questions:

\medskip
\begin{compactitem}[\labelitemi]
\item Does sharing the stack improve resource efficiency?
  (\autoref{subsec:reso_eff})

\item Can fine-grained scheduling and resource accounting ensure
  isolation of tenants despite sharing resources?
  (\autoref{subsec:perf_iso})

\item How close can optimized one-shot virtualization performance get
  to native un-virtualized stacks?
  (\autoref{subsec:virt_overheads})

\item Does \sys scale to serve many guests?
  (\autoref{subsec:scalability})

\item Does \sys improve VM performance in oversubscribed machines?
  (\autoref{subsec:oversubscription})
\end{compactitem}

\paragraph{Testbed.} We configure two identical machines as client and
server.
They are directly connected with a pair of 100\,Gbps Mellanox
ConnectX-5 Ethernet adapters.
Both machines have two Intel Xeon Gold 6152 processors at 2.1\,GHz,
each with 22 cores for a total of 44 cores and 187\,GB of RAM per
machine.
We run Linux kernel 5.15 with Debian 11.

\paragraph{Baselines.}
As baselines for comparison, we use two existing network stacks, the Linux network stack, and the optimized TAS TCP stack.
Depending on the configuration, we run these bare metal, or in
QEMU/kvm virtual machines with virtio-net vNICs connected to OvS.
We configure OvS with the DPDK backend and use vhost-user between
QEMU and OvS for optimal baseline performance.
%
%
For \sys containers, we directly mount the \sys Unix socket.

\paragraph{Focus on VMs.}
For most of our evaluation we focus on \sys with virtual machine
guests, rather than container.
The dominating fast-path interaction performance is identical
between \sys VM guests and container guests, while some slow-path
interactions in the VM case are more expensive than for containers
(\autoref{subsec:virt_overheads}).
At the same time we found \sys to provide higher relative benefits
when comparing to existing container stacks than compared with VM
stacks.
Thus, \sys with VMs provides a conservative evaluation and performance
comparison.

\subsection{Sharing the Stack Improves Efficiency}
\label{subsec:reso_eff}
We begin by measuring resource efficiency in guest workloads.
For this we provision up to four guest VMs, each with a Memcached~\cite{software:memcached}
or Nginx~\cite{software:nginx} server responding to
requests generated by up to four clients running the Memtier ~\cite{software:memtier} benchmark
tool for the Memcached setup and wrk~\cite{software:wrk} for Nginx.
Each client uses four threads to open a total of 200 connections.
We record the per/core efficiency as more VMs and clients are added
to the system
and show how siloed stacks reduce their efficiency because of the
extra fast-path cores taken up by the network stack in each VM.

As a baseline, we use separate TAS network stacks in each guest
connected to OvS on the host (OvS-TAS).
For the baseline we provision each guest with five cores, and configure
the TAS instances to use one fast-path core and the OvS instance to
use three fast-path cores.
For \sys we instead provision each guest with four cores, and assign
three fast-path cores to \sys.

\autoref{fig:reso-eff} shows the per-core aggregate
request throughput across all guests.
We obtained throughput numbers by
dividing the aggregate throughput by the number of fast-path
cores used by \sys and the baseline (TAS fast-path cores in VM and OvS polling cores).
\sys sees its resource efficiency increase because adding VMs increases the throughput.
This increase slows down as the fast-path cores in \sys
reach saturation around 3 VMs.
OvS-TAS sees a decrease in efficiency as more VMs are added to the system
because an extra core is used by the TAS stack in the guest VM, in addition
to the polling cores used by OvS. Our results show that sharing the
stack allows \sys to pool
resources and thereby significantly improve overall system efficiency.

\subsection{Fine-grained Scheduling Isolates VMs}
\label{subsec:perf_iso}

Next, we evaluate \sys ability to isolate guests despite sharing
a network stack and underlying resources.
To that end, we evaluate two main performance metrics, latency and
throughput, for a "victim" guest while a separate aggressor guest
attempts to introduce performance interference.

We evaluate two different forms of interference, by separately varying
the number of aggressor connections and the size of the aggressor
messages.
For the former the aggressor uses a fixed message size of 64 bytes, and for
the latter a fixed number of 500 connections.
The victim uses one connection
with 64 B messages for the latency measurements, and 500
connections with 64 B messages for the throughput measurement.
The victim uses a single core VM, while we provision
the aggressor VM with a core for every 500 connections.
Both victim and aggressor use the RPC echo server.

We compare this workload across different system configurations.
\sys with two fast-path cores, OvS-TAS with one additional
fast-path core per guest VM for the TAS instance, the guest Linux
stack with OvS with no additional guest cores.
Finally, we also compare to native TAS by running victim and aggressor
as separate processes on the host connecting to the same TAS instance
with two fast-path cores.
We use the timely~\cite{mittal:timely} congestion control algorithm in
\sys, OvS-TAS, and TAS.
In all cases VMs, processes, and network stacks are pinned to
dedicated cores and \sys equally divides resources for each guest
by setting the same value of $w_g$ for all guests.

The results in \autoref{fig:perfiso} confirm that \sys's fine-grained
isolation retains tail latencies below siloed OvS-TAS,
while improving victim throughput.
TAS without isolation increases tail-latency significantly
as the aggressor's message size increases.
TAS incurs tail latencies above \sys and OvS-TAS because of
the lack of isolation mechanisms based on resource usage.
For example, at 2500 aggressor connections \sys achieves a 99p latency
of 60\,$\mu$s, OvS-TAS's 98\,$\mu$s,and TAS's 276,709\,$\mu$s.
The benefits of fine-grained scheduling also hold when comparing
median latencies of the baselines.
The \sys victim achieves 40\,$\mu$s 50p latency when the aggressor
VM sends 1024\,B messages, while the TAS and OvS-TAS clients achieve
1461\,$\mu$s and 45\,$\mu$s 50p latencies.

We measure similar results with the victim's throughput.
TAS sees worse throughput as the aggressor VM increases
the number of connections or message size.
With \sys, the victim maintains similar throughput as the aggressor
seeks more resources.
For 2500 aggressor connections, \sys achieves 34\% higher throughput
than OvS-TAS.
